abstract: This study examines gender differences in generative AI adoption through two preregistered experiments at a top business school in Norway. The authors find a substantial gender gap: male students are 25% more likely to be high AI users, with the gap widest among highest-performing women. A survey of 1,134 managers shows acquiring AI skills would enhance job prospects, especially for top female students currently avoiding AI.
keyFindings: Among 595 business school students in Norway, male students were 25% more likely to be high AI users
The gender gap was widest among the highest-performing female students
Female students were more likely to view AI use as 'cheating' and less likely to persist when tools did not deliver on first try
When AI use was explicitly allowed, the gender gap completely closed — over 80% of both men and women intended to use AI
Top female students with AI expertise were rated higher by managers than those without, while male candidates did not receive the same premium
methodology: Two preregistered survey experiments. Study 1: 595 students at NHH (Norwegian School of Economics). Study 2: 1,134 managers across industries that typically hire NHH graduates. Includes causal evidence on policy interventions (explicit permission vs. bans).
qualifiers: Sample is from a single elite business school in Norway; may not generalize to broader populations. Student adoption patterns may differ from workforce adoption. Cultural context (Norway) may influence gender dynamics differently than other countries.
